interviewQuestions.question: How do you evaluate a search ranking model end to end?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate offline and online evaluation, because they answer different questions and neither alone is sufficient before shipping. Offline: score against labeled relevance judgments with NDCG@k as the primary metric, since it's position-aware and rewards getting the *best* result near the top rather than just having relevant items somewhere in the list — plain regression metrics like RMSE don't apply here at all, because the model's job is getting the order right, not predicting an exact relevance number. I'd also track MAP for a more holistic view of whether relevant results keep appearing throughout the list, and Precision@k specifically for the top few slots, since search UIs have limited visible slots and users rarely scroll — a model that's excellent at rank 20 but weak in the top 3 is failing at the part users actually see.

Offline metrics are proxies, not ground truth — the relevance labels themselves can be stale, inconsistently judged, or biased toward what was clickable in the past rather than what's genuinely most relevant now. So I'd follow with an online A/B test measuring real user behavior: click-through rate, dwell time, and ultimately the downstream business metric the ranking is supposed to drive (conversion, task completion), comparing the new ranker against the current production baseline on live traffic.

The reason both stages matter: a ranker can improve NDCG on the offline labeled set while making real users worse off, if the labels don't fully capture what users actually want in the live distribution of queries — offline is the fast, cheap pre-ship gate, online is the actual proof it helps.

**Testing:** whether you know regression metrics don't apply to ranked output, and that offline metrics alone — however good the NDCG number — aren't sufficient evidence before shipping.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Evaluating a search ranking model end to end

interviewQuestions.question: You're comparing two regression models and one has lower MAE but higher RMSE than the other. Which one is actually better?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
There's no universally correct answer — it depends on how you actually feel about large errors versus small ones, and the two metrics disagree here precisely because they weight errors differently. MAE treats every unit of error the same regardless of size — a model with many small errors and MAE treats a miss of 2 as exactly twice as bad as a miss of 1. RMSE squares errors before averaging, so a miss of 10 contributes 100 times as much as a miss of 1 to the sum — it disproportionately punishes large individual errors, even rare ones, far more than proportionally.

So a model with lower MAE but higher RMSE than another is telling you something specific: it's probably making mostly small errors that on average beat the other model, but it also has some individual predictions that are wildly off — occasional big misses that don't show up much in MAE's evenly-weighted average but dominate RMSE's squared sum. The other model, with higher MAE but lower RMSE, is likely more consistently mediocre — no huge individual misses, but a higher baseline error across the board.

Which one is "better" depends on the actual cost structure of the application. If an occasional catastrophic miss is genuinely much worse than many small errors — a pricing model where one wildly wrong estimate causes a bad business decision — I'd pick based on RMSE and investigate those large-error cases specifically. If errors of any size are roughly equally costly and I just want lower typical error, MAE is the more honest reflection of what I care about, and I'd pick the lower-MAE model. I would not pick based on an average of the two rankings — that's not a principled choice, it's avoiding the actual decision the cost structure demands.

**Testing:** whether you understand the different error-weighting behind MAE and RMSE well enough to interpret a disagreement between them, not just define each in isolation.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Interpreting a MAE vs RMSE disagreement

interviewQuestions.question: Your recommendation model has excellent per-item AUC but the product team says the actual recommendation lists look mediocre. What's the disconnect?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
AUC and NDCG are answering genuinely different questions, and a model can excel at one while doing poorly at the other — that's almost certainly what's happening here. AUC measures, across all items independently, how well the model separates relevant from irrelevant ones in general — it's a per-item, order-agnostic classification signal computed by comparing many random positive/negative pairs. A model can have excellent AUC because it's very good at telling relevant apart from irrelevant *in aggregate*, while still being sloppy about the *specific ordering* within any one user's list — putting the third-best item at position 1 and the best item at position 4 barely dents overall AUC (which doesn't care about within-list position at all) but is exactly the failure NDCG is built to catch, since NDCG explicitly discounts relevant items by how far down the list they land.

Concretely: a model could correctly rank "relevant" above "irrelevant" the vast majority of the time across all users and items (driving strong AUC), while consistently getting the *relative order among the several genuinely relevant items* wrong for any given user — and since users mostly look at the top 3-5 slots, that specific failure is exactly what the product team is seeing as "mediocre lists," even though the underlying classification signal is strong.

The fix is to stop treating AUC as sufficient evidence of ranking quality and add NDCG@k (and ideally Precision@k for the visible slots) as the primary metrics the team optimizes and reports — AUC can stay as a useful secondary diagnostic for the underlying relevance model, but it was never the right metric to judge list quality by.

**Testing:** whether you can explain why AUC and NDCG measure structurally different things, not just that "ranking needs different metrics."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Reconciling good AUC with mediocre-looking ranked lists
